description: About 60 content creators were invited to a Downing Street reception last month, with videos from the event, including of Burnham DJing, subsequently
body: About 60 content creators were invited to a Downing Street reception last month, with videos from the event, including of Burnham DJing, subsequently emerging online.In one video, Max Balegde, whose real name is Max Trobe, mouths the words "bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets", using audio from a meme that is trending online.Badenoch said the words used were "so offensive that I will not repeat them in this House". "Disgusting and pejorative comments about women's private parts, obscene language that referred to white women as cheap meat."This is grotesque. Labour MPs constantly tell us about their commitment to fighting violence against women and girls. Those MPs were silent yesterday, I won't be."Burnham said the Tory leader was "right to call out that, because it was not acceptable" but he would "not apologise" for engaging with young people."She sneers at TikTokers, she sneers at influencers," he added, accusing Badenoch of "having nothing positive to say to the country" and of "constantly talking it down".The two leaders continued the argument throughout their weekly Commons clash, with Burnham saying "it's true I have spoken to influencers, and then I have to come to this House, with the opposite of influencers".Badenoch said the PM preferred to "take questions to people dancing around Downing Street", a reference to a video of another content creator dancing through Number 10 and down the stairs in an attempt to recreate a scene from the film Love, Actually.This prompted Burnham to make a jibe about "lockdown parties" in Downing Street during the Covid pandemic.Responding to the row about his now-deleted TikTok video in an Instagram post on Tuesday, Balegde said: "My content is always meant to be silly, fun, and light-hearted."If anybody was offended by that video, I sincerely apologise."But he said "nobody was offended for weeks until revolting right-wing people tried to put this disgusting narrative on it"."And if anybody then looks at the video and is offended, I get that. So hence why I took it down because I think that is disgusting."Videos which were filmed inside the Downing Street premises were recorded on government phones.Attendees at the event have confirmed they had to hand personal devices in and were given a phone and a camera to film with, with the footage they recorded sent to them after the event.Artist Sophie Tea, who has more than 1.3 million followers on TikTok, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme she had been "excited" to be invited to the Downing Street reception, describing it as a "privilege". "I believe in the democratization of information and I think this opportunity was perfect for me to be able to understand more what's going on. "Number 10 is meant to represent the whole country and the more people feel like they belong there, the better."She said she was looking to use her social media platform to "communicate to the UK some of the brilliant things that are happening in government".Asked if she was being used by the government, she said "absolutely" but it was "mutually exploitative" because, as an independent artist, she had used it to "prop up my own value".This isn't the first time influencers have been invited into Downing Street. Former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak was interviewed by content creators during his time in office.Nor is it the first time they have descended onto Number 10 en masse, with the first content creator reception taking place under Sir Keir Starmer's leadership in 2025.Content creators are also regularly invited to press conferences and government briefings, including an event at Number 11 Downing Street on the day of the Budget last month.Writing on X, Luke Tryl, the UK director of pollsters More In Common, said it was "sensible" for Burnham to use influencers to reach a wider audience and it was "helping the PM seem in touch". But, he added, the PM's "biggest weakness" was being seen as a "people pleaser" and he should also do "non-softball interviews with traditional scrutiny media" to help tackle that.

title: Zoe Kleinman: Nobody is irreplaceable - unless you're Jensen Huang
description: Remember the tech boss and his head of HR, both married to other people, who were caught on camera at a Coldplay concert with their arms wrapped aroun
body: Remember the tech boss and his head of HR, both married to other people, who were caught on camera at a Coldplay concert with their arms wrapped around each other?Their horrified reaction went viral, and the pair both resigned. Astronomer, the firm where they both worked, said their actions had fallen short of its standards.Compared with the scandal which has engulfed Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang in recent weeks, that Coldplay kiss cam moment now feels rather tame.Huang admitted to having had an affair, reportedly with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy. There were suggestions that she may have been involved in smuggling Nvidia chips into China, in breach of a US export ban. Concerns about national security had reached the desk of US President Donald Trump. There were other stories about some of Huang's relationships with female colleagues.For most of us, that would without question amount to instant, and irreversible, dismissal.But while Huang briefly left the company, he was just as swiftly reinstated, and welcomed back with open arms. As I watched footage of him being greeted with cheers, applause, high fives and a big hug back at the company's HQ on Monday, I wondered how many disgraced bosses would kill to be in his shoes."Imagine being that Coldplay CEO reading all the comments on here about how it's OK if you're actually a good enough CEO," quipped menswear writer Derek Guy on X, external.So, the US AI sector relies on Nvidia, Trump is determined that the American AI industry needs to be the best in the world, and Huang is the only leader the company has ever known.  He's been at the helm for 33 years and he's a computer scientist himself, renowned for being very hands-on with the development process. (Whether the boss's input is always wanted is another matter, but it's always there.)Working for Huang isn't easy.Long hours are normal and negative feedback is often given in front of everyone else. When he wants something to happen, he doesn't stop until it does: one of his early ideas was to halve the chip production cycle, in order to get one step ahead of the competition with their longer lead times for orders. Lots of experts told him it couldn't be done. Until eventually, they did it.Not only does Huang have technical expertise, he's also a charismatic figurehead, representing Nvidia at events around the world in his trademark leather jacket, rubbing shoulders with world leaders, royalty, and fellow tech bosses. For many, he's become something of a cult figure. Nvidia sometimes sells limited edition clothing at conference pop up stalls. A jumper featuring a cartoon image of Huang costs $178 (£137).

schema.headline: Zoe Kleinman: Nobody is irreplaceable - unless you're Jensen Huang

title: I'm A Celebrity: Hundreds complain after Mariella Frostrup called AJ Odudu 'aggressive'
description: Frostrup replied that she thought being labelled "aggressive" was "a woman thing more than anything else"."I think women who speak their mind and are
body: Frostrup replied that she thought being labelled "aggressive" was "a woman thing more than anything else"."I think women who speak their mind and are forthright, that's 'aggressive', whereas a man who speaks his mind and is forthright is a 'strong man'," she said, but added that "I totally get that there's more" when race is involved.Odudu responded: "I do definitely see your point and agree with it, but those words stick as well. Those words can stick for us. The moment passes for you and it doesn't pass for me.""But hopefully it has?" Frostrup asked.Odudu replied: "Well, I wasn't being aggressive, so it shouldn't have been there."Signs of friction resurfaced when Frostrup told Odudu that "you don't take an apology well".Odudu replied that "of course" she had accepted her apology, before Frostrup accepted that "it's really important to me to understand why it's triggering".Odudu added: "It's good you asked, but it's a strong word to use in casual scenarios, particularly towards black women.""Good to know," Frostrup concluded.An ITV statement said: "The production monitors everyone in camp 24/7 and if at any time we feel someone has overstepped the line by using inappropriate language or displaying unacceptable behaviour, we would take steps to intervene and speak to everyone involved."The duty of care for our contestants is of the utmost importance to us. We take the welfare of the celebrities very seriously and have measures in place to ensure they are supported at every stage of the process: before, during and after filming."

schema.headline: I'm A Celebrity: Hundreds complain after Mariella Frostrup called AJ Odudu 'aggressive'

title: Blade Runner 2099: Hunter Schafer's series 'not just about AI'
description: "What does it mean to be human?" is a question that's always been at the heart of Blade Runner.The first film in the series, released in 1982, depicte
body: "What does it mean to be human?" is a question that's always been at the heart of Blade Runner.The first film in the series, released in 1982, depicted a technologically advanced yet dystopian version of Los Angeles in the then-distant future of 2019.While the movie's flying cars haven't - quite - materialised yet in the real world, Blade Runner's themes of technological progress and the threats it poses feel just as relevant.At least that's what the cast and crew of Blade Runner 2099, a new TV series set in the same universe, are hoping.BBC Newsbeat spoke to stars Hunter Schafer, Lewis Gribben and Dimitri Abold, plus showrunner Silka Luisa, to ask why they think themes of artificial consciousness and existential threats still resonate.The original Blade Runner, directed by Sir Ridley Scott, is considered a sci-fi classic that had a long-lasting influence on the genre.It told the story of Detective Deckard, played by Harrison Ford, who hunted down synthetic humans known as replicants.Schafer says her first exposure to the series was actually marketing for Blade Runner 2049 - the film sequel starring Ford and Ryan Gosling in 2017."I never thought I'd have the opportunity to make an addition to the world," she says."And so when that opportunity came along, I was quite thrilled."Blade Runner 2099 is set 80 years after the original film, and portrays a Los Angeles where replicants have taken over.Schafer plays Cora, a fugitive human forced to team up with replicant Olwen (played by Michelle Yeoh), as she tries to track down an artefact that could save humanity.The series lands at a time when there are disagreements about the nature of the threat AI could pose to humans. "I think it's particularly relevant right now, especially for the youth and young people who are inheriting a world that's asking a lot of the same questions that the show asks," says Schafer."I think that's timely and hopefully helpful to some degree."But Blade Runner 2099 isn't "necessarily about just AI", says showrunner Luisa."It's this bigger question of what is the world going to be in 15 years and how can you plan for it?" she says.The first Blade Runner also touched on themes of corporate greed and environmental damage, which are evident in the new series.Luisa hopes the theme of a future that "is not going to be what you were promised" resonates with viewers today."The idea that you were born into a world and you thought you were expecting certain aspects of your life just to roll out," she says."That system is collapsing. And so what will be your place in whatever comes next?"Blade Runner 2049 won awards and scored well with reviewers, but reports suggested it didn't hit box office targets.This was partly blamed on marketing for the film trying to appeal more to existing fans than new ones - so what would the cast say to get younger viewers on board?"It's just a very rich world," says Gribben, who plays Cora's younger brother Elias. "It makes you want to learn more."Gribben also points out that Blade Runner 2099, which employed "hundreds of artists and craftspeople" according to its makers, is a celebration of traditional film-making despite its themes."I think a lot of people crave human stories," he says."They crave new kind of worlds and new things."And I think studios will rely more on technology to make better-looking movies, but they won't have that soul."Abold, who plays Cora's human ally Bebeto, says one of the show's key messages is about "the connections that you make". "And the connections that you make are the foundation of humanity," he says."Because at the end of the day, all we have is ourselves and each other, right? And that's what feeds any human emotional experience."

schema.headline: Blade Runner 2099: Hunter Schafer's series 'not just about AI'

title: Russia's own figures show it has lost nearly 500,000 people in Ukraine war
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Russia does not provide numbers of its fallen soldiersByOlga Ivshina and Yaroslava KiryukhinaBBC Russ
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Russia does not provide numbers of its fallen soldiersByOlga Ivshina and Yaroslava KiryukhinaBBC RussianUpdated 1 hour agoAt least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by the BBC.The leaked Rosstat data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia, and show the high cost paid in human life in a war that Vladimir Putin had assumed would last only days but is now almost five years old.BBC Russian has had access to more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, after a hack by Belarusian group Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow.Russia's statistics agency admitted to a cyber-attack, but denied any protected information had been leaked. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Wednesday that only Russia's defence ministry could officially report data on losses: "I suggest no other data be taken into account." The defence ministry has not released any official casualty figures for several years.Together with independent Russian outlet Mediazona, BBC Russian has compared the Rosstat data with its own list of confirmed military deaths, pulled from open sources since the start of the invasion, and it has found matches for 90% of the records.Military experts estimate that the BBC's list of 290,012 deaths, gleaned from official reports, social media, new memorials and graves, may account for 45-55% of the true death toll, which would range from 527,295 to 644,471.The records show that 65% of 18 to 24 year-olds in Russia who lost their lives in 2025 died in the war. For those aged 25-34 the number was 59%. Only among 45 to 54 year-olds does cardiovascular disease claim more Russian lives than the conflict.The data also reveal the extent of losses in specific areas of Ukraine. Some 20,000 Russian soldiers died fighting for control of 10 Ukrainian villages whose combined pre-war population was 12,000.During the fight for one small village called Andriivka, south of the town of Bakhmut in Donetsk region, 1,122 Russians lost their lives. Before the war 74 people lived there.Russia does not give public figures for losses sustained since the war began in February 2022. And two years ago Rosstat stopped publishing data of deaths from external causes, which was used to gauge the extent of military losses.For example, only 70% of deaths we have established of soldiers from the occupied regions of Donetsk and Luhansk in eastern Ukraine who fought in the Russian army  were accounted for in the Rosstat files.Overall, the Rosstat dataset confirms the trends that we have observed with our own count.Ukrainian losses were last put at about 50,000 by President Volodymyr Zelensky in July 2026, but another list based on open sources by the anonymous UA Losses website puts the figure at 115,952.How we came to a figure near half a millionThe Rosstat dataset contains no names but does include ages, places of residence, places of death and also circumstances of death.We have filtered the records first by location, leaving only Ukraine as well as Russian border regions that saw incursions by the Ukrainian army.Next, we identified 425,174 entries explicitly indicating a military-related cause of death, such as explosions or shrapnel during combat operations.As this count could include civilians, we filtered out women as well as men outside the 18-65 age group. And if someone lived and died in the four Ukrainian regions occupied by Russia, we excluded them as a possible civilian – unless he had a record of military service attached to his entry.Another 14,093 entries were identified by looking at employment, and 51,067 were recorded in the database as deceased on the basis of a court ruling. This often happens when a soldier goes missing in a combat zone for more than six months and their body has not been recovered.Again, we filtered out civilians by only counting deaths in the war zones in Ukraine and Russia.According to BBC Russian's analysis of the leaked files, in the first year of the war the average age of those killed was 34. By 2025, as prisoners and contract soldiers entered the ranks, it had risen to 40 (38 according to our own list).Some of Russia's poorest regions in Eastern Siberia account for a disproportionately large share of the losses. Men from Tyva, Buryatia and Zabaykalsky Krai are 20-25 times more likely to die in the war than residents of the biggest cities of Moscow and St Petersburg.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesIn most regions, the distribution of deaths based on Rosstat data differs from that in the BBC's list by just a few tenths of a percentage point.At least 5,017 foreigners are among those who died fighting for Russia, according to our analysis of the Rosstat files, including 1,031 Uzbeks and 720 Tajiks. We have left out Ukrainians from this count to avoid including civilians.This is a conservative estimate as dual nationals are listed as Russians in the database, and there is no reference to North Koreans who died repelling the Ukrainian incursion into Russia in 2024.The BBC identified 2,304 North Korean soldiers who died there by analysing satellite imagery and official photographs of a newly built memorial in Pyongyang.The leaked Russian statistics may not be complete but taken in conjunction with BBC Russian's own work they are significant. In the context of a war that has lasted four years and 10 months, these are high numbers for Russia, when compared with the Soviet war in Afghanistan that ended in 1989.In that 10-year war, an estimated 15,000 Red Army troops died, and an estimated one million civilians were killed.Additional reporting by Ilya Barabanov

schema.headline: Russia's own figures show it has lost nearly 500,000 people in Ukraine war

title: EA adds AI-generated John Motson to FC 27 video game
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, John Motson was a legendary football commentator who covered 10 World Cups, 10 European Championships and 29
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, John Motson was a legendary football commentator who covered 10 World Cups, 10 European Championships and 29 FA Cup finals for BBC SportByTom GerkenTechnology reporterFootball game EA Sports FC will feature the digitally recreated voice of the late commentator John Motson, Electronic Arts has exclusively told the BBC.Motson, who died in 2023, was the main commentator for BBC Sport for decades - and performed the same role for the video game series during the 90s and 00s.It is the first time the hit series, formerly known as Fifa, has featured a deceased commentator.With the permission of his widow and his son, Motson's voice has been synthesised using a combination of old recording sessions and generative AI. It will become available in FC 27 on 26 November.The legendary commentator died aged 77 in February 2023 - several months after the launch of ChatGPT and the massive growth of AI it set in train. Fred Motson told the BBC it "means an awful lot" to have his dad's voice in EA Sports FC once again."I grew up with Fifa," he said. "I always used to tell my parents that I needed the latest console for Christmas because otherwise dad couldn't see how the game worked."Electronic Arts, which was bought for $55bn (£42bn) in August, told the BBC it paid Motson's family for the rights to use his likeness and recreate his voice, but would not disclose the financial terms of the deal.Figure caption, WATCH: The new John Motson commentary in EA Sports FC 27 - and how it sounded back in Fifa 1998John Motson was the first commentator for the series, appearing on games from Fifa 96 up to Fifa 2005. He later made a brief cameo in Fifa 19. "While he completely understood when they went in a different direction, I think he really missed it after he left the game and it felt like a bit of an end of an era," his son said.EA told the BBC the studio would not have included Motson in the game unless they had permission from his family."There was no way we would have moved forward with this in any way, shape or form if they weren't fully on board," said Mat Prior, senior game design director at EA Sports FC."At the outset we wanted to pay tribute to to Motty as the commentator and as this emotional connection - he was the very first voice of our game - so we really wanted to do him justice and bring him back." He explained that Motson's voice in the game was a combination of old lines he recorded over the years and AI - tech which he said was "the only way" to make it happen, as they don't have recordings of him talking about modern players like Bradley Barcola and Chloe Kelly.Figure caption, Gazza's tears, Radford's screamer & the Crazy Gang - 5 of Motty's bestMotson's son Fred said he believed his dad would have "absolutely" wanted to be involved in the game after his death."My dad was the least technological person in the world," he said. "Till his dying day, he had a typewriter on his desk."So I don't think he would have quite understood what the AI was doing technologically - but I think, on the other hand, he was always really keen to get involved in these kinds of projects."But Peter Caulfield, founder of Save Our Voices Now which campaigns against AI voice cloning, expressed some disquiet about the project, and the fact Motson had been unable to consent to it."If someone has signed a deal allowing their likeness to be used after they die, I have no issue with that," he said. "But in life or in death, unless you have specifically agreed to it, AI cloning of any kind should not be allowed. "Being a family member shouldn't automatically give you that right either."One of the main arguments against the use of generative AI in video games is that it can replace humans - something that EA was keen to argue against."From a gaming standpoint, it's something we've used for many years - like machine learning to help drive animation systems and so on and so forth," Prior said. "It's not there to replace commentators in any way shape or form... there's certainly no future plans to replace anyone with AI." Derek Rae, who has been a commentator in EA FC for several years, said the tech could make things easier, but he still spent a long time recording dialogue in studios."It's quite a lot of days in the course of a year," he said. "So it might be two or three times a month that we do it in season for the game, which is typically sort of November time through until May."The more creative things have to be done with the human voice because they have to have the personality, sometimes a little chuckle thrown in the middle of a sentence or a little idiosyncrasy," he said."But when it comes to the more normal features in a video game, for example, routine surnames like Smith and Jones and Brown, that's something that AI can probably accomplish quite easily."Image source, EA SportsImage caption, Josko Gvardiol tackling Jamal Musiala in FC 27 - perhaps examples of some less routine surnamesRae said he was excited about the Motson project - but wasn't convinced he would follow suit."If we're being modest, we might say, well, no, I don't want to inflict my voice on the next generation."He told BBC News it was something he would need to "think about" it but added: "I'm hopefully many years away from having to make a decision like that."

schema.headline: EA adds AI-generated John Motson to FC 27 video game

title: Hera spacecraft investigates damage at asteroid "crash scene"
description: Close-up images to be revealed of asteroid deliberately hit to test ability to protect EarthImage source, ESAImage caption, The Hera spacecraft will s
body: Close-up images to be revealed of asteroid deliberately hit to test ability to protect EarthImage source, ESAImage caption, The Hera spacecraft will study the 150m-wide (490ft) asteroid called DimorphosPictures will be released later of damage to an asteroid which a spacecraft was deliberately crashed into four years ago as part of a test of Earth's defences.In what may sound like the plot of a disaster movie, Nasa's Dart spacecraft smashed into the space rock in 2022 to knock it slightly off course.The Nasa craft was obliterated on impact. Now, a European Space Agency (ESA) mission called Hera is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision - with the first images set to be released later on Wednesday.The asteroid poses no threat, instead this was the first ever test of our planetary defences to see what action we could take if a space rock was heading for our planet."Hera is a sort of Inspector Columbo going back to the crash scene to investigate what is the outcome of this impact," said Patrick Michel, principal investigator of ESA's Hera mission.Image source, NASA/Johns Hopkins APLImage caption, This was the last image from Dart before it crashed into Dimorphos in 2022The crash test focussed on a pair of asteroids: a larger one called Didymos - about 730m (2,400ft) wide - which is orbited by a smaller rock called Dimorphos, about 150m (490ft) wide.The Dart spacecraft targeted Dimorphos, hurtling into the rock at 22,000km per hour (14,000mph). Images beamed back showed the asteroid's rocky surface coming ever closer until the feed cut out on impact.It was such a big smash-up that the trail of debris, measuring about 10,000km long (6,200 miles), was spotted by telescopes on Earth and in space.The crash showed it was possible to change the path of the smaller asteroid.Before the collision it took Dimorphos 11 hours and 55 minutes to orbit around Didymos. After the Dart crash, the duration of its orbit had shrunk by about 33 minutes.But the arrival of the second spacecraft, Hera, will help scientists to answer many more questions."Dart exploded in the asteroid, and therefore we don't have the information of what is its final state," explained Michel."The impact could have left a crater - and if it is the case, we need to understand the size and the depth. Or [the impact] may have entirely reshaped the asteroid."Image source, NASA/Hubble Space TelescopeImage caption, A 10,000km-long (6,200 miles) debris trail was spotted by the Hubble Space Telescope The Hera mission will spend the next year studying Dimorphos, and take a look at Didymos too.The spacecraft is packed with instruments, and it also has two small shoe-boxed sized satellites onboard, which can study the impact site up close, and then later land on the asteroid.A key task is to measure the mass of Dimorphos, to work out how effective the spacecraft's shove was.This information would be vital if we ever spotted a space rock that was on a collision course with Earth."It would help us to predict what would happen if we had to hit another asteroid," said Prof Simon Green, a planetary scientist who is on Hera's science team."We [could] measure its properties and say: 'Well, we need this mass of spacecraft, travelling at this speed, this early, in order to deflect it enough so that it misses the Earth'."Image source, ESAImage caption, Hera has already sent back an image of Didymos with Dimorphos in the background Asteroids pose a significant threat to our planet.The biggest, which measure more than a kilometre across, could cause global devastation.  But medium-sized asteroids around the same dimensions as Dimorphos could wipe out a city."We all know what happened to the dinosaurs, right? And we don't want that to happen to us," said Carolyn Ernst, Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, who works on both the Dart and Hera missions."The good news for us is that there are far fewer potential threats out there in the Solar System than there were millions of years ago. But there are objects out there."She said the biggest asteroids have been spotted, and none are heading to Earth."The smallest stuff isn't too much of a threat because our atmosphere protects us," she added."But there's a size range in the middle where we don't know where all of them are, and it could, if impacted, cause problems for humanity.  And if we can find out about that and know about that, well, we sure as heck would want to try to stop that."Image source, ESAImage caption, Hera has two small satellites onboard to study the asteroid up closeScientists want to gather as much intelligence as they can about space rocks - to make us as well equipped as possible to deal with whatever the Universe throws at us.A new mission is launching in 2027 to track potentially hazardous asteroids: a space telescope called the Near-Earth Object (NEO) Surveyor.There are also more visits planned to asteroids, including to one called Apophis, which is about 450m (1,480ft) long.Apophis was discovered in 2004 and it was initially thought it might hit the Earth as early as 13 April 2029.But now scientists understand its orbit better, and say it won't hit us for at least the next 100 years.  Instead of a crash in 2029, it will fly just 32,000km (20,000 miles) above our surface.This will give scientists the rare chance to study a space rock up-close.Two spacecraft will head to Apophis, including Nasa's Osiris-Apex (which previously grabbed a sample from another asteroid called Bennu) and Ramses, a joint mission between ESA and the Japanese Space Agency (JAXA).

schema.headline: Hera spacecraft investigates damage at asteroid "crash scene"

title: UK sent sex offender refugee to African country in undisclosed deal
description: The UK forcibly resettled a refugee and convicted sex offender in an African country with which he had no connection, in a deal not disclosed to the U
body: The UK forcibly resettled a refugee and convicted sex offender in an African country with which he had no connection, in a deal not disclosed to the UK Parliament or the local community.The man, who was from Sri Lanka and had a history of severe mental illness and suicide attempts, took his own life months after arriving in Eswatini.The BBC has obtained a copy of the draft deal between the two governments, in which the UK pledges to cover the costs of his resettlement for up to three years.The UK government was finalising plans for 35-year-old Kishanth Peramalya to live there permanently when he died.Migration experts told the BBC this was the first known case of the UK government forcibly resettling in such a manner a refugee permanently overseas.In 2024, the Labour government scrapped a controversial plan to send asylum seekers with pending claims to Rwanda. Now it wants to send failed asylum seekers overseas to third countries when they cannot be sent to their home countries, but is yet to announce any deals. Last week, five EU countries reached a deal to send people whose claims have been refused to Rwanda. The Eswatini deal raises questions about how much the UK government should disclose about such arrangements, and how it protects both the people it sends overseas and the communities that receive them.The UK government told the BBC that protecting the British public was its priority and that it "continue[s] to work with the Eswatini authorities in relation to this case".Peramalya's family is demanding answers about his treatment, while critics in Eswatini have accused Britain of using their country as a "dumping ground".As a teenager, Peramalya had been tortured and sexually abused by officers in the Sri Lankan military and was later diagnosed with PTSD. During his detention on Diego Garcia, his mental health deteriorated, according to court papers. He suffered from depression and anxiety, and repeatedly attempted suicide. UN inspectors who came to the island raised concerns over the conditions he was being kept in.While there, he committed a series of crimes, including assault and arson, during two suicide attempts, and spent 24 weeks in prison. He was also convicted of four counts of sexual assault for which he received a suspended prison sentence.In December 2024, most of the Sri Lankan asylum seekers were allowed to enter the UK but ministers refused to let Peramalya join them because of his crimes. He remained on Diego Garcia.The High Court upheld the UK's refusal to admit him, in part because of the risk he posed and because ministers were making genuine efforts to find somewhere else safe for him to live. Court documents, seen by the BBC, show the UK approached more than 20 countries and could not secure an agreement.Then, in February 2026, the US began using its military base on Diego Garcia in its war with Iran. The island authorities began withdrawing non-essential personnel.At the end of March, the Maldives offered to take Peramalya for 30 days. He was transferred there before being sent on to Eswatini, formerly known as Swaziland.At the time of his death, the British and Eswatini governments had been finalising the agreement for Peramalya to live there permanently, with the UK to pay for the "reasonable costs" of his accommodation, healthcare, and other support for up to three years.The document does not specify a total cost or explain how the two governments would manage the risks Peramalya posed to himself and others. But it explicitly acknowledged he required support that would meet his basic needs and protect his physical and mental health, and wellbeing.Peramalya's family has told the BBC he was initially placed in an isolated guesthouse on his own.Speaking from India, his sister said the family had not been aware of the plan to make his transfer permanent, and that his mental health had worsened while in the country.She said he would call her four times a day. "My brother did not want to go there at all," she said. "He couldn't manage being there alone, he was very lonely." The family also said it had been unaware of sexual offences committed by him.He initially saw a psychiatrist weekly, she said. Later, after his mental health declined, he had daily appointments, and an attendant was brought in to prepare his food.On 13 September, he took his own life.The UN's refugee agency, which had previously raised concerns about Peramalya's condition on Diego Garcia, said it was "deeply saddened" by his death and stressed that refugees being transferred to other different countries must be protected."UNHCR recognises that asylum seekers and refugees may, in certain circumstances, be lawfully transferred to a third country. However, this requires that specific safeguards are in place and those conditions are fulfilled in practice."Peter Walsh, of Oxford University's Migration Observatory, described the case as "highly unusual". "In most cases, people with criminal convictions who cannot be returned to their home country would simply remain in the UK. Third countries are generally quite reluctant to accept foreign national offenders," he said.It is unclear how Britain chose Eswatini, but the kingdom had already agreed to accept US deportees under President Trump's wider programme of sending migrants to countries across Africa and Latin America. In 2025, the Trump administration paid Eswatini $5.1m (£3.9m) to accept up to 160 people.Melusi Simelane, of the Southern African Litigation Centre, who is challenging the US deal in court, said migrant transfers were putting pressure on his country's limited resources."Our healthcare system is crumbling, not to mention our mental healthcare, so it is a big ask to bring people into our society who need a lot of support," he said."Africa is becoming a dumping ground for the world's unresolved problems."Zakithi Sibandze, of the Eswatini Rural Women's Assembly, which campaigns to protect women and girls, said it was "very painful" that a sex offender had been relocated to her country."Why did they think it was okay to send him to Africa?" she asked. "The UK seems to be saying it is fine for people to commit crimes against women in poor countries."Earlier this year, the UN's special rapporteur on migrants' rights, Gehad Madi, urged governments to publish the terms of their migration arrangements with other countries and subject them to parliamentary and public oversight. "Strengthening transparency is essential to reduce human rights risks, ensure accountability and uphold the rule of law," he said.Neither the UK nor Eswatini authorities answered the BBC's questions on the circumstances surrounding Peramalya's resettlement, but a spokesperson for the British government said: "Keeping the British public safe will always be our first priority, and we will continue to take the decisions necessary to protect the British people. That includes taking steps to ensure high-harm foreign criminals cannot enter the UK."Additional reporting by Alice Cuddy and Swaminathan Natarajan

schema.headline: UK sent sex offender refugee to African country in undisclosed deal

title: Energy bills will soar - here's how you can save energy to ease the pain
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Keeping yourself warm by wearing thick clothes, using blankets and having hot drinks can help reduce heating
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Keeping yourself warm by wearing thick clothes, using blankets and having hot drinks can help reduce heating billsByCost of living correspondentUpdated 2 hours agoEnergy bills will soar by 26% in the new year as the war in Iran pushes up wholesale prices. Typical household bills will rise by £37 per month as Ofgem's latest price cap comes into force from January to March, but experts say it is possible to keep rising bills in check. Here are four areas to consider ahead of the increase.1. How you can save energyOfgem's price cap, as well as suppliers' fixed deals, set a limit on the price of each unit of energy, not the total bill.So, you pay for what you use. Millions of people have cut back on their energy consumption during years of relatively high prices.With the unit price of gas, in particular, set to soar, experts say you should take a fresh look at your energy use and renew good habits.Research foundation Nesta suggests:turning down the flow temperature on a combi boiler - usually indicated by a radiator icon, to make it operate more efficientlyturning off the pre-heat facility on some combi boilers, which would have kept some water heated up when not in useturning down the thermostat one degree, although 18C is the recommended minimumclosing all curtains at nightlowering radiator valves outside of the living roomturning off the heating before AprilThese are small changes but - alongside washing clothes at 30C, blocking draughts and batch cooking - they can reduce energy use and bills.2. Pay by direct debitOfgem says about five million people still pay their bill when it arrives every three months, rather than receive a monthly bill often initially based on an estimate.Taking regular meter readings, or having a smart meter, while paying by monthly direct debit solves that problem. Paying by direct debit costs significantly less than by so-called standard credit - typically £138 cheaper a year.Customers on prepayment schemes  - usually people on low incomes struggling to pay bills - used to pay a higher rate than others, but now they pay slightly less than the capped direct debit variable rate.Various deals may rely on paying by direct debit or having a smart meter.3. Consider switching to a fixed rateMoving to a fixed energy tariff means the price you are charged per unit of gas or electricity does not change every three months, although the total bill will still vary depending on how much energy you use.The trouble is that it is very difficult to work out whether a fixed deal is a good deal at the moment, for those renewing fixed deals or looking for one for the first time.Some fixed deals are available at unit prices below the next forecast price cap level. But should energy prices fall sharply then a longer-term fix might not seem such good value compared with the price cap.So consumer group Which? also recommends paying close attention to any exit fees when picking a fixed deal. If variable prices fall below your fixed rate and you want to get out of it before the end of your agreement period, you may have to pay a hefty sum.Before you fix, consumer website MoneySavingExpert advises you look at all the deals available, not just what your own supplier is offering.4. Check what financial support you can getThe government will give a £100 payment to millions of homes to help cover winter energy costs. It will go to homes in council tax bands A to D in England, with the equivalent expected in Scotland and Wales.There are also a range of other forms of support specifically for people on low incomes.This winter anyone on means-tested benefits will get £150 off their electricity bill. Your supplier will apply the discount automatically unless you are in Scotland, where you will need to contact your energy company to ask for the help.Some people will also be eligible for a Cold Weather Payment, external and most pensioners will receive the winter fuel payment.Beyond that, most energy suppliers offer hardship grants for people struggling to pay their bills and the government's Fuel Direct Scheme, external can help you repay energy debt.You can get more advice from Ofgem, external, Citizens Advice, external, or your own energy supplier. Trade body Energy UK has a list of support schemes, external.People on low incomes may also be eligible for grants to help with insulating their homes, and there are local schemes offering grants for solar panels, heat pumps and the like.But if you are hunting around for grants, watch out for scams pretending to be official money-off schemes.Get in touchHow is the cost of energy affecting your quality of life? What questions do you have?

schema.headline: Energy bills will soar - here's how you can save energy to ease the pain

title: Why tiny cars are taking off across Europe
description: Selena Buse, 16, reverses her Citroën Ami out of a parking space and heads off past the school playground. Heads turn. The Ami looks pretty remarkable
body: Selena Buse, 16, reverses her Citroën Ami out of a parking space and heads off past the school playground. Heads turn. The Ami looks pretty remarkable. Futurist or like-a-toaster depending on your point of view. But it's changed her life."I got it because I really needed it to get to school. And I use it to visit friends on the weekends. It's indispensable in rural areas like where I live," she says.In France, you can drive a car like this from the age of 14 with a road safety certificate and eight hours training. In Italy too.In Germany and Spain it's 15, in the UK 16, external. Because they are classed as motorised quadri-cycles. Four-wheel mopeds in other words.Registrations have risen from about 13,000 in 2019 to around 25,000 last year in France.In Europe, sales have gone from 30,000 to 60,000 in the past five years. And the Ami, launched in 2020, has really changed the image, with teenagers who now account for a quarter of all mini-car sales.In Selena's very small Citroën, we are soon rolling along at the top speed of 45km/h (28mph). For other road users, no-licence cars like this can seem like mobile traffic calming."When I'm on faster roads and there's a lot of traffic the cars behind me sometimes honk their horns but I can't go any quicker!" Selena says.Another local Daniel Laprès, who drives a micro-car made by French firm and market-leader Aixam, tells me he actually pulls over to let the cars behind pass.He and his wife moved from Paris to this country village two years ago. Of Canadian nationality, he didn't swap his foreign licence for a French one in time and lost the right to drive. That didn't matter much when he was in Paris. Like many Parisians he didn't need a car. He used public transport. But that's not possible here."We tried living off of taxis and it was in the end a disaster. Then we heard about how you could drive without having to have a licence, and it was the exact solution to our problem. Cheap, inexpensive to operate, basically no administrative formalities, you get insurance."However, Laprès feels less safe in his small car. "They're little more than tin cans on wheels, right? I mean, you're not going to be driving fast, but someone else could be." These cars are forbidden on motorways. But even on medium-fast roads, being considerably slower than the average vehicle can be a problem."You go on national highways at your risk and peril. I did it once and I will never, ever do it again. On those roads (speed limit 110km/h), everybody is passing you, including the biggest trucks. And they come at you very fast from the rear, so it's scary," Laprès says.Daniel is 77 so fits in with the long-established market for these cars: older people living in the countryside.Traditionally the market also included quite a few people who'd lost their licences, often because of drink-driving offences. But the launch of the electric Citroën Ami in 2020 changed the customer profile and the product."The launch of the Ami was the beginning of the transformation of the sector, with more and more electric models coming on to the market. In 2026, more than 67% of new licence-free cars are electric," says Marie-Laure Nivot, market analyst at AAA Data.This tendency was encouraged by stricter EU regulations on motorised two-wheelers that had been the vehicles of choice for European teenagers until then."It proved too costly for manufacturers to apply the new EU rules, so mopeds and small scooters have almost disappeared from the market since 2020 and licence-free cars have taken their place," Marie-Laure Nivot says.Tiny car sales rose strongly till 2024 although they have flattened since in France with the withdrawal of subsidies for electric models.Curiously, the arrival in this niche market of a giant competitor in the shape of Stellantis brand Citroën was actually good news for existing French manufacturers like Aixam and Ligier."We're specialised in this niche market and we're very good at what we do, but of course, we didn't have the communication strength of a multinational like Stellantis. They helped us to make people understand that it was possible in France to drive this product from 14-years-old, in Germany from 15-years-old. They gave a lot of visibility to our market," says Aixam sales and marketing director Tom Faget.Aixam has invested €30m (£25m; $33m) in expanding its production capacity in France. And its sales are growing in other European countries, even as the French market slows.Meanwhile, the competition is producing increasingly sophisticated minicars - some costing as much as a small conventional car. At Ligier, marketing director Romain Illegems says the biggest change is in who's buying them."We've gone from mobility that was imposed on people to mobility that people choose. Before, these vehicles were something you used because you absolutely needed to get around, because there was no public transport, or because you didn't have a licence."Today, teenagers are choosing them instead of scooters or mopeds, because they're safer and offer better protection from the weather. Young people now account for 40% of our customers."There are limitations, of course. Just two seats, a maximum speed of 45km/h and no motorways. But for Selena, who rents her Ami for €60 a month, plus insurance, it's a small price to pay for independence.

schema.headline: Why tiny cars are taking off across Europe

title: A question of trust in the NHS could be Swinney's most dangerous political moment
description: Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, John Swinney has asked the government's top civil servant to review how correspondence is handledByScotl
body: Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, John Swinney has asked the government's top civil servant to review how correspondence is handledByScotland political editorUpdated 7 hours agoAt its heart this is a story about trust.Trust in doctors and other health professionals at NHS Grampian to provide the highest standards of treatment and care. Trust in their managers to effectively deal with problems when they arise.And trust in the Scottish government to step in if that does not happen.What we have learned about the operation of NHS Grampian in the last two weeks raises huge questions in all of these areas.First we had a scathing report by the watchdog Healthcare Improvement Scotland, which found serious shortcomings with NHS Grampian's leadership and oversight of clinical governance.There was particular concern about patterns of repeated and avoidable harm, and the board's ability to learn from serious adverse events.The Scottish government has sent in a support team to help the current management at NHS Grampian make improvements.Questions have been raised about the suitability of some of those appointed to carry out this work given problems they have faced in their own areas of responsibility.The watchdog's report was followed by a powerful intervention from a surgeon-turned-whistleblower who works at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary.Dr Mohammed Habib said he had been raising serious concerns about liver and pancreatic services at the hospital for 10 years.He released a previously unpublished review from 2022 that looked at 45 patients in the care of this specialist unit over the previous seven years.It said that 31 had died, and 19 of them were considered to have died of avoidable consequences of surgery or intervention.This is the key detail in this story.Nineteen people died and their deaths were potentially avoidable.This finding was not made public by NHS Grampian or those in the Scottish government who knew about it.This is where this story becomes political - because Dr Habib tried to get the attention of ministers.He raised his concerns with the Scottish government including, he said, writing to the first minister on three occasions.At Holyrood question time, John Swinney acknowledged that the issues raised were of the "gravest concern".He said Dr Habib's messages had received "appropriate responses" from officials.It seems they directed him to a national whistleblowing service and to the police.Image caption, Dr Habib said he wrote to the first minister on three occasionsThis is what, in my view, makes this potentially the most dangerous political moment for John Swinney since he took over as first minister in 2024.A surgeon writes to him because 19 people may have died unnecessarily as a result of how they were treated by the NHS and nothing seems to happen.We have since been told that Swinney's office did not make him personally aware of this correspondence.That in turn raises questions about the operation of the highest political office in devolved Scotland.After two decades in power would the SNP administration not have an established system for deciding what should and should not be seen by the first minister?And if a pattern of seemingly avoidable deaths in the NHS is not serious enough to be escalated to the top then what is?The potential for political disasterSwinney seemed to recognise the inadequacy of his parliamentary answers fairly quickly.Soon after question time his team said he had asked the Scottish government's top civil servant to review how correspondence is handled.This too was only the beginning of a realisation within government that this had the potential to develop into a political disaster.By Saturday, Health Secretary Angela Constance had decided to announce an independent review into who knew what and when, what they did with the information - and why.Before the weekend was out, she was on BBC Scotland's The Sunday Show promising 100% transparency and accountability.She seemed angry to have been left carrying the can for something that should have been dealt with more robustly at a far earlier stage.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Angela Constance said the inquiry's findings would be published in fullWe have now learned that the review will be led by an experienced King's Counsel, and the likelihood is that they will come from outside Scotland.Constance has said that any clinical input they receive will definitely come from outside Scotland.The KC will be able to scrutinise the actions of current and former ministers, civil servants, and those working in the health service.Constance said their findings would be published in full and that any urgent matters that arise during the review should be reported directly to relevant bodies.The minister also said it was "categorically false" to say that no action was taken following the 2022 report, which was drawn up by University of Edinburgh Professor Stephen Wigmore.Constance said liver and pancreatic surgery was suspended for a time, then resumed under the professor's supervision until he was satisfied it could continue without his oversight.It was stopped again on at least two further occasions and patients requiring complex surgery have been transferred to NHS Lothian since early this year.More scrutiny in parliamentIt has been reported that former Health Secretary Humza Yousaf and current chief medical officer Sir Gregor Smith were aware of the 2022 review.Yousaf has made clear he supports full scrutiny and "further dramatic action" in NHS Grampian. Sir Gregor has yet to make any public comment.The review process will not necessarily contain this crisis of confidence.More patients and their families may come forward to share their experiences, or perhaps others within NHS Grampian will choose to speak out.The involvement of the campaigning lawyer Aamer Anwar, who is working with Dr Habib, increases the likelihood of this type of follow-up.There will undoubtedly be further parliamentary scrutiny, with the possibility of key figures being called before a Holyrood committee.It is worth remembering that the police are also taking an interest and have yet to determine whether or not a formal investigation is merited.Some have hinted at the potential need for a judge-led public inquiry, although these tend to take a very long time and cost a huge amount of money.There are already three health-related public inquiries into Covid handling, major hospital building projects in Glasgow and Edinburgh, and botched brain surgery in Dundee.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The deaths of 19 people at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary could have been avoidedThere is a clear determination by government and opposition at Holyrood to see a much faster remedy to the complexity of problems in NHS Grampian.A turnaround in healthcare delivery and management in north east Scotland is being pursued alongside radical plans to overhaul how the NHS is run across the country.The government is proposing to merge the existing network of regional health boards into just two for the whole of mainland Scotland.There will be those who argue that this provides an opportunity to create a more robust system of supervision and a more rapid response when things go wrong.Others fear that this kind of centralisation could result in local deficiencies being overlooked.This could become an important feature in the debate over NHS reform.In the meantime, the Scottish government has to convince the public and political rivals that it has got a grip of what's happening in NHS Grampian.That seems essential if patients are to have confidence that they can place their trust in the vital services it provides.

schema.headline: A question of trust in the NHS could be Swinney's most dangerous political moment

title: 'I only use the washing machine on a Sunday' - how we're keeping our energy bills down
description: ByDaniel Thomas and Anuk WeerawardanaBusiness reportersUpdated 1 hour agoDomestic energy prices will soar by 26% in January under the regulator Ofgem'
body: ByDaniel Thomas and Anuk WeerawardanaBusiness reportersUpdated 1 hour agoDomestic energy prices will soar by 26% in January under the regulator Ofgem's new price cap, pushing up bills for millions of households across England, Scotland and Wales.With household budgets already under pressure, finding ways to reduce gas and electricity costs has become increasingly important. But how much difference can simple changes really make?The BBC spoke to three people about what they're doing to keep their energy costs down.'We power down at peak times'Image source, Kelly Anne HarveyImage caption, Kelly Anne Harvey uses electric blankets and portable oil radiators in some rooms to save on the central heatingLike many people, Kelly Anne Harvey, a building surveyor from Cleveleys near Blackpool, is worried about her energy bill going up next year.The 44-year-old, who is married with a five-year-old son, has a combined household income of £60,000. She currently pays about £154 a month for gas and electricity on a standard variable rate with Octopus, but is looking for a fixed-rate deal to offset the rise.The family fell into arrears on their energy bills a few years ago and Kelly says she won't let it happen again. To control her costs she pays by direct debit, which spreads her payments and is typically £138 cheaper a year than paying on receipt of a bill. The family uses electric blankets and portable oil radiators in some rooms so they don't have to turn the central heating on as often. They also take part in Octopus's energy saving scheme, which rewards customers who use less electricity at peak times, such as early evenings, with a free hour of energy at the weekend. "On Sunday we'll turn on the dishwasher, tumble drier, washing machine and maybe even charge our electric cars," says Kelly.'We've turned the heating down by 2.5C'Image source, SuppliedImage caption, Stacey says she keeps the curtains closed "to keep the heat in" and her daughters wear thermal clothingStacey, 40, a single mother from Bristol, says dealing with rising energy costs has felt like a "battle" recently and she's worried about 2027. The office worker, whose daughters are aged 10 and 12, is on a fixed-term tracker tariff with E.On Next, which charges rates set below the quarterly Ofgem price cap. She expects to pay £1,800 for energy this year, up £400 on last year. Stacey, who is part of the Changing Realities project at Glasgow University, which documents life for people on low incomes, has tried a number of things to control her energy costs. She's turned her central heating down from 22C to 19.5C, bought electric blankets and pays her bills by direct debit. She also leaves her curtains shut to "keep the heat in", while her daughters wear thermal clothing if it gets chilly in the house. The family is also using less hot water."I've got girls and they're growing up and they want to spend loads of time in the shower [but] it's just not possible."'I order heating oil in bulk'Image source, SuppliedAround 1.5 million households in the UK rely on heating oil for heating and hot water, and their costs have already soared in the past year due to disruption in global oil markets."When I first moved here two years ago you could get a litre of heating oil for 50-60p," says Bradley Knowles, 32, who lives in a barn conversion with his husband, mother and sister in rural Lincolnshire. "At the height of the Iran war it went up to £1.20 or £1.30 and now it's stabilised at around £1."To cut costs, the finance worker orders oil in bulk, buying 1,000-1,500 litres, preferably in the summer months when prices are lower. He also tries to order a few weeks in advance to avoid expensive next-day deliveries. Bradley uses comparison sites to see which local suppliers offer the cheapest oil and puts money aside each month so he can always afford his orders. Oil-powered boilers may take time to heat up, but Bradley advises against leaving them on all day as that can be very expensive. Instead, he uses an electric tank to store his warm water and tops up the heating in parts of the property with electric radiators.   Additional reporting by Kris Bramwell & Bernadette McCague. Get in touchWhat are you doing to cope with rising energy bills?

schema.headline: 'I only use the washing machine on a Sunday' - how we're keeping our energy bills down

title: Footballer Raheem Sterling given suspended sentence for dangerous driving
description: Witness Christopher Jennings called 999 after driving alongside Sterling's car on the M25, and "he was shocked by what he saw", Jones said, and made c
body: Witness Christopher Jennings called 999 after driving alongside Sterling's car on the M25, and "he was shocked by what he saw", Jones said, and made clear "he sighted the defendant inhaling from the balloon".Fiona Jennings – driving on the southbound M3 – described the driving as "absolutely horrendous" and "swerving in and out of lanes", the court heard.The court heard Sterling strayed into the central reservation of the M3, exited at junction 4A, and veered off the A327, crashing into a metal gate near a layby.His vehicle sustained "substantial damage to the tyres and bodywork and was no longer capable of being driven", the court heard.Sterling was taken to Basingstoke police investigation centre by officers, where he disclosed he had a "problem with nitrous oxide", said Jones.He complied with an impairment test, but for a blood sample, Sterling asked to obtain legal advice before making a decision.In the police sergeant's view "he was deliberately failing to provide a clear answer".Sterling was later interviewed by police with legal representation present where he accepted he had been the driver and provided no comment answers about the driving.Defending Sterling on Wednesday, Jason Bartfeld KC said there was no dispute that this was a "top category case" because of prolonged driving and "at times" serious impairment which would have been short periods within the driving.But the defence did not accept the damage to the car was serious and said there was "confusion" over the failure to provide a specimen.

schema.headline: Footballer Raheem Sterling given suspended sentence for dangerous driving

title: Beauden Barrett: All Blacks great close to stunning Bristol Bears move
description: New Zealand great Beauden Barrett is close to agreeing a deal to join Bristol Bears in what would be one of the highest-profile signings in Prem histo
body: New Zealand great Beauden Barrett is close to agreeing a deal to join Bristol Bears in what would be one of the highest-profile signings in Prem history.The 35-year-old, who is widely considered one of the best All Blacks of all time, won his 150th international cap in Saturday's defeat by England in Twickenham.It is understood he is in discussions about joining Bristol on a two-year deal after the 2027 Rugby World Cup.Barrett is also the subject of interest from clubs in France as he plots the final stages of his illustrious career. An announcement on his future is expected in the coming weeks.Bristol have yet to comment on the situation, but sources close to the deal feel the Bears are in a strong position to sign the 2015 World Cup winner. New Zealand's international season finishes this weekend with a rematch against England in the Nations Championship third-place play-off (Saturday, 16:40 GMT).As a new addition to the Prem, Barrett's salary would sit outside the cap as a designated marquee player. While he will be 36 after next year's World Cup in Australia, Bristol are confident the back still has plenty to offer both on and off the field.Barrett came through the ranks at Wellington-based Hurricanes, before joining the Blues in 2020, while he has also had stints in Japanese club rugby.A move abroad after the World Cup would close the door on his illustrious international career, with eligibility rules preventing New Zealand from picking overseas-based players.He would leave as one of the greatest All Blacks in history, and is closing in on Sam Whitelock's all-time caps record (153).Bristol have made a handful of big-name signings in the past, such as New Zealand and Tonga winger Charles Piutau and Fiji talisman Semi Radradra.If the signing is completed, Barrett would link up with Wales superstar Louis Rees-Zammit in the Bears backline.

schema.headline: Beauden Barrett: All Blacks great close to stunning Bristol Bears move

title: She spent decades as an FBI agent and this is the case she could not let go
description: Image source, Submitted photoImage caption, Jane Collins spent 30 years with the FBI - but no case stuck with her quite like the case of Nexus, Michae
body: Image source, Submitted photoImage caption, Jane Collins spent 30 years with the FBI - but no case stuck with her quite like the case of Nexus, Michael Donovan and Richard MooreByRobin Levinson-KingJane Collins had spent 30 years as an FBI agent, but there was one case that haunted her long after retirement.Michael Donovan was a fraudster, former minister and multimillionaire she had pursued for years, and even in her retirement she could not escape him.He was regularly featured in the news and on the radio, appearing as a spokesperson for a number of causes, from migrant rights to anti-racism and justice reform.He and his husband, Richard Moore, lived about an hour's drive from her, in Augusta County, Virginia, on the edge of the Appalachian Mountains.Together they owned a business, Libre by Nexus, which had made more than $200m (£152m) from migrants seeking release from US immigrant detention centres - but it was a scam, government regulators said.To Collins, they were the ones who got away.They were fined $811m for conning detained migrants, but the scams didn't stopShe had investigated Nexus from 2016 until her retirement from the FBI in 2021. But the only federal criminal charges either faced - after almost six years of her investigation - was a tax charge against Moore.So when Collins left the bureau, there were still a few strands left of her investigation that she could not let go - like the case of Zach Cruz, the brother of the man who killed 17 people in Parkland, Florida.They had fronted his $500,000 bail bond, personally picked him up from jail, given him somewhere to stay, and made media appearances on his behalf.Investigators later found they also took $400,000 from him, proceeds from his late mother's life insurance. Last month, the pair were found guilty of stealing it - with Collins playing a key role as a witness during the trial.Collins told the BBC in her only interview about the case that she saw it as her final chance to face them in court. "It means something when people are held to account," she said.A paper trailCollins says she was still a young girl when she first thought about joining the FBI."I've always been very interested in justice, making things right, and I think all of those things just fell into place," the 64-year-old recalls from her home in Charlottesville, Virginia, where a picture of her late golden retriever named Yogi hangs on the wall and a vintage car is parked in the driveway.She was accepted to Quantico, the FBI training academy, soon after finishing university, and began to climb the ladder at the bureau, conducting surveillance on suspected Russian spies and crack dealers. In the late 1990s, she began working more on white-collar crimes, which really excited her - "much to my surprise," she adds. What she liked about these cases was the paper trail, and the way they presented themselves as puzzles to solve."There's a lot more in those cases that are concrete. As we say, documents don't lie," she says. "It was more challenging."It also changed her perspective on crime, and victims. Although there was no trail of blood, there was an undeniable ripple from the fraud to the people and families hurt by it."People getting defrauded of money, some people their life savings," she explains. "There's a lot of psychological issues that go with that for a victim. They have been duped, so they're very hard on themselves."An opportune appearanceWeeks after his older brother gunned down 14 students and three staff members at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland,  Zachary Cruz went to the campus to "reflect on the school shooting and soak it all in".But when police found him there skateboarding, they arrested the then 18-year-old, charged him with trespassing and put him in jail. On the heels of his brother's massacre, a judge set his bail at $500,000.His friend called Nexus, looking for help to get him out. But Donovan and Moore did more than that - not only did they pay his bail, but they picked Cruz up from jail and took him to a hotel room.Cruz later told the court that when he met them for the first time, it felt "like a movie".During dinner that first night, the couple asked Cruz if he wanted to move to Virginia and work for Nexus.The Florida judge overseeing his probation called it a "wonderful opportunity".Soon he was living with them, and sharing in their media spotlight. Donovan and Moore accompanied him on interviews where the young man spoke about trying to understand his brother's crimes.The couple even helped produce a short-lived online reality show called "Being Zach Cruz", which chronicled what it's like to be the brother of a famous killer. "It was not ordinary," he later said.According to Moore and Donovan, in an interview with the BBC in 2022, Cruz had become part of their family. They called him their "son" and said they had spent lavishly on his pursuit of a skateboarding career.But they were deeply in debt, fighting off creditors - and the IRS. And through it all, Collins was doggedly on their tail.Image caption, Zach Cruz, left, was taken in by Michael Donovan, centre, and Richard Moore, right, after his brother killed 17 people in Parkland, FloridaDonovan and Moore had spent their wealth extravagantly - a fleet of luxury vehicles, a $500,000 wedding and a million-dollar self-published book titled Not Free America: What Your Government Doesn't Want You to Know.But they owed millions to several state insurance boards, which had fined them for operating an unlicensed bond company. They owed a former business partner, RLI Insurance, millions for their failure to pay back bail that was lost when clients skipped court. And Moore owed more than $3m to the IRS.Prosecutors alleged it was this tax debt that spurred Moore and Donovan to dupe Cruz out of his inheritance. Donovan declined an interview, through his attorney.Collins initially focused her investigation on Libre by Nexus, and whether the company had broken any laws.But her case took a turn when she received a tip that Donovan and Moore may be personally exploiting Cruz.Bank records showed that $428,000 - the insurance money Cruz was entitled to after his mother died - was transferred into a joint account held by Cruz and Moore, and then into Moore's personal account, in 2019, according to the county's search warrant.Collins tried to interview Cruz, who was still living with Moore and Donovan.Driving up to their house one evening, Collins says she saw an armed security guard stationed outside, while barricades blocked the entrance to the front door and driveway."People can't easily come and go," she thought to herself. Cruz never came to the door.A shadow of a doubtSince 2016, Collins had been working on the case in conjunction with the Internal Revenue Service and Homeland Security Investigations, which oversees immigration law. The agencies were investigating whether Nexus defrauded people and brought migrants illegally to work for their company, as well as the allegations involving Cruz's insurance money and tax fraud.But by the time she was due to retire, the federal prosecutor in charge of the case had narrowed the focus to just tax fraud, which he passed onto another prosecutor.Collins was disappointed.Ultimately, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau - a federal agency with the power to bring civil, but not criminal, cases to court - took legal action against Nexus, leading to an $811m judgement against the company.The agency provides a much-needed service, helping to pursue corporations when other avenues have failed, said Ted Mermin, executive director of the Berkeley Center for Consumer Law & Economic Justice.To bring a criminal case, "you have to show that beyond a shadow of a doubt they violated the law", he said.A civil case, on the other hand, only needs to show that it is more likely than not that they violated the law.Figure caption, 'My brother, the Parkland gunman'Meanwhile, Collins was running up against the clock: the FBI has a mandatory retirement age of 57, and she had already been extended. She retired in the summer of 2021 at the age of 59.A few months later, Cruz, Donovan and Moore sued her, alleging she had "conspired to create a fake 'joint investigation'" with a local agency, and that her career was "cut short after she violated department policies and/or laws in connection with her rogue investigation".The bureau's attorney repudiated those claims, and a federal judge dismissed the case. The lawsuit did little to dissuade Collins, who brushed it off as "frivolous"."I was not intimidated by them," she told the BBC. Through his attorney, Donovan declined the BBC's request for comment. Moore, who is serving a seven-year prison sentence for filing a fraudulent Nexus tax return, did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.Before she left the bureau, Collins sat down with her bosses and the agent assigned to take the case over from her, she said. She still had hope that it would be prosecuted.But more than a year went by, and there were no charges.The house of cardsIt seemed, at least for a while, that her case was finished. Then, in October 2022, local police and Virginia State Police stormed Moore and Donovan's home in Fishersville, and their offices in Verona.It was not the feds, as Collins had hoped. But this was still a chance at holding the men to account.They seized laptops, mobile phones, body cameras and thumb drives. Donovan and Moore were arrested and charged, and then released on bail.Evidence of the raid was still clear in the shattered glass of the front door, when the BBC went to Nexus offices to interview the couple several days after police stormed the property.In the interview, Donovan and Moore said they had not taken advantage of Cruz and had done nothing wrong.Zach, who was still living with them at the time, told the BBC he had spent all his inheritance willingly. But he is no longer living with the couple, and appeared as a witness for the prosecution during the trial.After Collins retired from the bureau in 2021, she began working for a state agency. She plans to retire for good in a few years, when she hopes to spend more time with her husband and three children and travel around the world.Looking back, she thinks of this chapter at the end of her career in federal law enforcement as discouraging. She had wanted to declare "case closed" years ago."I enjoyed my career immensely. I wouldn't trade it. I felt like I made a big difference in a lot of ways," she says. "But this case, it caused me a lot of frustration."Still, she says, she feels grateful that someone did take this case on.When she heard the jury had convicted them on all counts, she thought: "Finally, justice"."It had been a long time coming," she said. "But we needed to wait until the house of cards fell down."
